claims.text: The intervention uses in-situ substrate preheating at approximately 150–200 °C.
The intervention uses a defocused laser beam with a power density of approximately 150–250 W/cm².
Combining substrate preheating with reduced laser power density will significantly reduce residual thermal stresses relative to conventional high-power, room-temperature processing.
The combined intervention will improve ductility relative to conventional high-power, room-temperature processing.
The combined intervention will improve strength relative to conventional high-power, room-temperature processing.
Adjusted scanning speeds under the reduced-power, defocused-beam condition can produce a stable, wider melt pool.
Reduced thermal gradients and slower cooling produce more uniform solidification.
More uniform solidification yields a fine-grained microstructure.
More uniform solidification minimizes contraction stress.
Preheating decreases the temperature differential between the melt pool and substrate.
A smaller melt-pool-to-substrate temperature differential reduces contraction stresses during cooling.
Lower, defocused laser input limits extreme localized thermal input.
Controlled melt-pool dynamics promote homogeneous solidification and mitigate residual-stress formation.
The intervention will produce a more reproducible microstructure than conventional high-power, room-temperature processing.
Conventional high-thermal-load processing with a room-temperature substrate typically produces steep thermal gradients and high residual stresses.
Conventional high-thermal-load processing typically degrades mechanical properties.
The specified processing window is applicable to miniature AlCrFeNiSi components, while changes in scale or geometry may require additional tuning.
